prompt: In a polymer made from a conjugated diene, double bonds occur along the chain once every how many carbon atoms?
explanation: Diene polymerization is a 1,4 addition, so each monomer unit adds four carbons to the chain and keeps one double bond: double bonds occur every four carbon atoms. That makes cis–trans isomers possible.

prompt: How does the growing chain add to each conjugated diene monomer during diene polymerization?

choices.text: By 1,4 addition, leaving a double bond between the monomer's carbons 2 and 3
By 1,2 addition, leaving a vinyl group on every other carbon
choices.why: Diene polymerization is a 1,4 addition of the growing chain to the monomer.

choices.text: By Diels–Alder cycloaddition, forming a cyclohexene ring
choices.why: Polymerization joins monomers end to end in a chain; it doesn't form rings.

choices.text: By adding to both double bonds, leaving no double bonds
choices.why: Each monomer unit keeps one double bond, so diene polymers have a double bond every four carbons.

explanation: Like simple alkenes, conjugated dienes can be polymerized, but the polymerization is a 1,4 addition of the growing chain to a conjugated diene monomer. A new double bond forms between the monomer's former carbons 2 and 3.

prompt: What can serve as the initiator (In) for diene polymerization?

choices.text: Either a radical or an acid
Only a radical
choices.why: An acid can also initiate the reaction; Exercise 14.6.2 is about acid-catalyzed polymerization of 1,3-butadiene.

choices.text: Only an acid
choices.why: A radical, as in ethylene polymerization, can also be the initiator.

choices.text: Elemental sulfur
choices.why: Sulfur is used afterward, in vulcanization, to cross-link the finished chains.

explanation: The initiator for diene polymerization can be either a radical, as occurs in ethylene polymerization, or an acid.

prompt: Natural rubber is a polymer of which diene?

choices.text: Isoprene (2-methyl-1,3-butadiene)
Chloroprene (2-chloro-1,3-butadiene)
choices.why: Chloroprene gives the synthetic rubber neoprene.

choices.text: 1,3-Butadiene
choices.why: 1,3-Butadiene gives polybutadiene. Natural rubber is made from isoprene.

choices.text: 1,4-Pentadiene
choices.why: 1,4-Pentadiene is not conjugated. Rubber is a polymer of the conjugated diene isoprene.

explanation: Rubber is a naturally occurring diene polymer of isoprene (2-methyl-1,3-butadiene), produced by more than 400 different plants. The major source is the rubber tree, Hevea brasiliensis, whose crude latex is harvested as it drips from a slice in the bark.

prompt: How does gutta-percha differ from natural rubber?

choices.text: Its double bonds are E rather than Z, and it is harder and more brittle
Its double bonds are Z rather than E, and it is softer
choices.why: Rubber's double bonds are Z. Gutta-percha is the E isomer, and it is harder and more brittle.

choices.text: It is made from chloroprene rather than isoprene
choices.why: That's neoprene. Gutta-percha is a naturally occurring isoprene polymer, the E isomer of rubber.

choices.text: It has no double bonds, because it has been vulcanized
choices.why: Gutta-percha is a natural isomer of rubber with E double bonds. Vulcanization adds sulfur cross-links; it doesn't remove the double bonds.

explanation: The double bonds of rubber have Z stereochemistry, but gutta-percha, the E isomer of rubber, also occurs naturally. Harder and more brittle than rubber, it is used in dental endodontics and as the covering on some golf balls.

prompt: Which monomer is polymerized to make neoprene?

choices.text: Chloroprene (2-chloro-1,3-butadiene)
Isoprene (2-methyl-1,3-butadiene)
choices.why: Isoprene gives natural rubber and synthetic polyisoprene.

choices.text: 1,3-Butadiene
choices.why: Neoprene contains chlorine; it is made from chloroprene, 2-chloro-1,3-butadiene.

choices.text: Vinyl chloride, H2C=CHCl
choices.why: Vinyl chloride isn't a diene. Neoprene comes from the conjugated diene chloroprene.

explanation: Chloroprene (2-chloro-1,3-butadiene) is polymerized to yield neoprene, an excellent, although expensive, synthetic rubber with good weather resistance. It is used to make industrial hoses and gloves, among other things.

prompt: What happens during the vulcanization of rubber?

choices.text: Heating with sulfur cross-links the chains through carbon–sulfur bonds
Heating with sulfur breaks the chains into shorter pieces
choices.why: Vulcanization joins chains with C–S cross-links, which hardens the polymer.

choices.text: Hydrogenation removes the double bonds from the chains
choices.why: Vulcanization uses elemental sulfur, not hydrogen.

choices.text: The Z double bonds are converted into E double bonds
choices.why: That would give gutta-percha. Vulcanization cross-links the chains with sulfur.

explanation: Natural and synthetic rubbers are too soft and tacky to be useful until they are heated with elemental sulfur. Vulcanization cross-links the chains by forming carbon–sulfur bonds, hardening and stiffening the polymer; the degree of hardening can range from tires to bowling balls (ebonite).

prompt: What lets rubber stretch and then return to its original shape?

choices.text: Double bonds kink the chains, which straighten when pulled, while cross-links stop them sliding apart
The chains are straight and nest tightly together, so they can't move
choices.why: The double bonds introduce bends and kinks that keep neighboring chains from nestling together.

choices.text: Stretching breaks the cross-links, which re-form when the tension is released
choices.why: The cross-links stay intact; they keep the chains from sliding over one another.

choices.text: Stretching converts the Z double bonds to E, and relaxing converts them back
choices.why: Stretching straightens randomly coiled chains. No cis–trans isomerization takes place.

explanation: The double bonds introduce bends and kinks that prevent neighboring chains from nestling together. When stretched, the randomly coiled chains straighten out along the pull but are kept from sliding over one another by the cross-links. When the tension is released, the polymer reverts to its random state.

prompt: Which repeating unit would you expect in a polymer made from 2-phenyl-1,3-butadiene?

choices.text: –CH2–C(C6H5)=CH–CH2–
–CH2–C(C6H5)(CH=CH2)–
choices.why: That would come from 1,2 addition. Diene polymerization is a 1,4 addition, which puts a double bond in the chain.

choices.text: –CH=C(C6H5)–CH=CH–
choices.why: Both double bonds can't survive. Each monomer unit keeps one double bond, between its former carbons 2 and 3.

choices.text: –CH2–CH(C6H5)–CH2–CH2–
choices.why: Polymerization doesn't remove every double bond; diene polymers keep a double bond every four carbons.

explanation: In 1,4 addition, carbons 1 and 4 of each monomer bond to neighboring units and a new double bond forms between carbons 2 and 3. The phenyl group on carbon 2 ends up on a double-bond carbon: –CH2–C(C6H5)=CH–CH2– (Exercise 14.6.1).

prompt: Natural rubber is a polymer of isoprene. How many carbon atoms are in each repeating unit of the rubber chain?
explanation: Each repeating unit comes from one isoprene molecule, 2-methyl-1,3-butadiene (C5H8): four chain carbons plus the methyl group, 5 carbons in all.
